h1: Olive Oil vs Sesame Oil: Two Strong Flavours, One Job Each
excerpt: Olive oil and sesame oil are both strong-flavoured, both used raw and both used to cook, and a lot of Malaysian kitchens already keep both. This is where each one wins, not which one replaces the other.
keyTakeaway: Olive oil and sesame oil are both strong, distinct-flavoured oils used raw and in cooking, but they rarely do the same job. Toasted sesame oil finishes a stir-fry or noodle dish off the heat; olive oil suits a raw drizzle or a moderate sauté. Most kitchens keep both rather than choosing one.

intro: Two oils with strong, distinct flavours turn up in a lot of Malaysian kitchens at once, and neither erases the need for the other.
This is where each one earns its place: flavour, toasted sesame oil against the light version, raw finish against cooking, and how olive oil fits a kitchen that already keeps sesame oil.

sections.heading: Two flavours that do not compete

blocks.text: Extra virgin olive oil tastes of the fruit it was pressed from — grassy, peppery or mild depending on the harvest. Sesame oil tastes of the seed: a deep, toasted, nutty note when the seeds were roasted first, or a lighter one from raw seeds.
That is the reason to keep both. A dish built around sesame oil's toasted aroma falls flat with olive oil in its place, and hummus wants olive oil's fruit and pepper, not a nutty note.

sections.heading: Toasted and light sesame oil are two different products

blocks.text: Toasted sesame oil is pressed from roasted seeds and comes out dark amber with a strong, unmistakable aroma — a finishing oil, not a cooking one. Light or raw sesame oil is pressed from unroasted seeds, pale and mild, and holds up better to heat.

items: **Toasted sesame oil** — dark, strongly aromatic, added at the end of cooking or as a raw finish.
**Light (raw) sesame oil** — pale, mild, closer to a neutral oil in a pan.
Buying 'sesame oil' without checking the label leads to a burnt dish or a bland one.

sections.heading: Poured on at the end, not cooked from cold

blocks.text: Toasted sesame oil is almost always finished rather than started: a few drops stirred through a stir-fry once the wok is off the heat, or drizzled over noodles just before serving. Cooked from cold, it turns bitter before the dish is done.

Olive oil works both ways: a raw drizzle carries its fruit and pepper, but it also takes a moderate sauté from the start — see [olive oil smoke point](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) for how much heat it takes.

sections.heading: Where olive oil fits a kitchen that already has sesame oil

blocks.text: Olive oil does not replace sesame oil in a kitchen that already keeps one — it does a different job. Sesame oil finishes a stir-fry with its own toasted note; olive oil finishes a salad or roasted vegetables with a grassy, peppery one.
Both earn a place on the same shelf. For which oil suits which dish more broadly, see [how to cook with olive oil in a Malaysian kitchen](/blog/how-to-cook-with-olive-oil-in-a-malaysian-kitchen).

blocks.text: Most of the choice comes down to timing: whether the oil needs to survive real heat in the pan, or whether its job is to sit raw on top of a finished dish.

sections.heading: How much of each you actually use

blocks.text: Toasted sesame oil is used a few drops at a time, so a small bottle lasts months. Olive oil is poured more freely and goes through faster once it earns a regular place in the same kitchen.

Arabian Village extra virgin olive oil comes in 250 ml and 500 ml, sold in Malaysia only through [Berkat Madinah Store](/shop) — two branches in Selangor, plus the seller's own Shopee and TikTok Shop counters. See [the products page](/products) for sizes and pricing.

Keep both bottles for what each does best: sesame oil, toasted especially, for a raw or barely-heated finish; olive oil for everything from a raw drizzle to a moderate sauté. Neither replaces the other — they are different tools for the same kitchen.

faqs.q: Can I use olive oil instead of sesame oil in a stir-fry?
faqs.a: Not for the finishing splash — sesame oil's toasted aroma is the point of adding it there. Olive oil can do the earlier cooking, but swap it in at the end and the dish loses the flavour it was built around.

faqs.q: What is the difference between toasted and light sesame oil?
faqs.a: Toasted sesame oil is pressed from roasted seeds — dark, strongly aromatic, meant for finishing off the heat. Light or raw sesame oil is pressed from unroasted seeds, paler and milder, and holds up to more heat in a pan.

faqs.q: Does sesame oil have a lower smoke point than olive oil?
faqs.a: This site has not published a smoke-point figure for sesame oil, so no number is claimed here. In practice, toasted sesame oil is treated as a low-heat finishing oil, not one poured into an empty hot pan.

faqs.q: Which oil is better for a stir-fry, olive oil or sesame oil?
faqs.a: Neither replaces the other in the same stir-fry. Sesame oil, usually toasted, is stirred through at the very end for its aroma; olive oil suits the earlier cooking or a raw finish on a different dish.

faqs.q: Can I mix olive oil and sesame oil in one dish?
faqs.a: Yes — a light sesame oil can carry the heat while a few drops of toasted sesame oil go in at the end for aroma, with olive oil kept for dishes built around its own fruity flavour instead.

faqs.q: Where can I buy Arabian Village olive oil in Malaysia?
faqs.a: Through Berkat Madinah Store's two branches in Selangor, or the same seller's own Shopee and TikTok Shop counters — see the shop page for details. There is no other legitimate seller of this brand.
